claims.claim: The working definition of community health, offered by McKenzie and colleagues in their 2005 textbook and reviewed by Goodman, Bunnell, and Posner in 2014, is that community health refers to the health status of a defined group of people and the actions and conditions, both private and public (governmental), to promote, protect, and preserve their health.

The World Health Organization's Health Promotion Glossary (1998) defines a community as a specific group of people, often living in a defined geographical area, who share a common culture, values, and norms and are arranged in a social structure developed over time.

A community is typically tied to a place and to shared norms, values, and organizations, whereas a population is any defined group of people, whether or not its members share a place, identity, or ties; community health organizes around place and relationships, while population health (the sibling topic) measures outcomes and their distribution across any defined group.

Community engagement is the process of working collaboratively with and through groups of people affiliated by geographic proximity, special interest, or similar situations, to address issues affecting the well-being of those people (CDC/ATSDR, Principles of Community Engagement, Second Edition, 2011).

The 10 Essential Public Health Services describe the public health activities that all communities should undertake; they include assessing and monitoring population health status, investigating health problems and hazards, informing and educating people about health, mobilizing community partnerships, and linking people to needed personal health services.

Public health promotes and protects the health of all people and their communities, aims to prevent illness and injury in the first place while health care treats people who are sick, and its workforce includes community health workers, health educators, inspectors, and public health physicians and nurses.

Implementing and using the results of community health assessments, that is, measuring and characterizing risk factors within and the health status of a community, is a core element in improving a community's health (Goodman, Bunnell, and Posner, 2014).

The U.S. field of community health is anchored in community intervention trials of the 1970s, including the Stanford Three Community Study, the North Karelia Project, and the Stanford Five-City Project, which worked to reduce risk-factor prevalence and disease burden at the community level.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The terms 'community' and 'population' are used loosely and sometimes interchangeably in public health writing.
positions: WHO's glossary and the community-health literature tie 'community' to a defined geographical area and shared norms, values, and identity.
The population-health literature defines a 'population' as any defined group of individuals, place-based or not.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the place-based, shared-norms community definition and states plainly that every community forms a population but not every population is a community; the outcomes-and-distribution lens is explicitly handed to the population-health sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The boundary between 'community health' and 'public health' is not sharp; some texts treat community health as a subset of public health practice, others as nearly synonymous.
positions: Goodman and colleagues note the meaning of community health remains difficult to fully define and to clearly distinguish from related areas of public health practice.
The 10 Essential Public Health Services describe activities 'all communities should undertake,' implying community-level practice is core public health work.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents community health as public health practiced at the local, street level — in a defined place, with local players — while public health is the broader field spanning all levels, topics, and approaches.

sourceRecords.title: What is "community health"? Examining the meaning of an evolving field in public health (Prev Med 2014;67 Suppl 1:S58-61)
sourceRecords.provider: Preventive Medicine (Elsevier), full text via U.S. National Library of Medicine PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Goodman RA, Bunnell R, Posner SF (CDC/HHS authors). Read 2026-08-22 as full text on PubMed Central (PMCID PMC5771402, open access). Supports: the McKenzie et al. (2005) working definition of community health ('the health status of a defined group of people and the actions and conditions, both private and public (governmental), to promote, protect, and preserve their health'); the Green and Ottoson (1999) community definition ('a group of inhabitants living in a somewhat localized area under the same general regulations and having common norms, values, and organizations'); community health assessments as a core element of improving a community's health; the 1970s community intervention trials (Stanford Three Community Study, North Karelia Project, Stanford Five-City Project); and the note that community health is hard to distinguish cleanly from related public health practice. Facts synthesized in original prose; the working-definition phrase is quoted briefly and attributed.
